title: What's the most beautifully written review you've read that wasn't written by Roger Ebert?

commenti.body:
Ebert was an amazing writer and indeed most of my choices would've been from him. 

  
I like Christy Lemire's review of Call Me By Your Name. [https://www.rogerebert.com/reviews/call-me-by-your-name-2017](https://www.rogerebert.com/reviews/call-me-by-your-name-2017)

This may go against spirit of your post (in that the following is the most hilariously excoriating review of an otherwise much-lauded film in a mainstream publication that I've ever seen - a rarity nowadays I think), but Nick Pinkerton's review of Beasts of the Southern Wild is something I find myself re-reading whenever it pops into my head.

[Full review here,](https://archive.org/details/Sight_and_Sound_November_2012/page/n83/mode/2up) choice quotes below;

>When I told a friend that I had discovered the worst movie of the year in Beasts, he replied: "The preview looks like what I imagine an Arcade Fire video would look like".  


>As protagonist Hushpuppy, eight-year-old Quvenzhane Wallis narrates in the cloudgazing, free-associative style of a Terrence Malick voiceover. Malick is a master who rarely rewards imitation, however, and no disciple has taken the Prometheus of Austin’s hard-won discoveries so far in the direction of parody as does Zeitlin (“Everything’s heart is heatin’ and squirtin’ and talkin’ to things in ways I can’t understand”). Wallis plays opposite Dwight Henry as her father Wink. She’s a first-time actress from Houma, Louisiana; he’s a local baker; both are terrible.  


> “Down with that hollow feeling!” begins the zesty ‘About’ section of Court 13’s website, which goes on to detail the group’s manifesto: “Court 13 values ‘do it yourself not as a matter of financial circumstance but as a spiritual requirement; each film poses huge, painstaking challenges that defy the gods, nature, and just plain common sense.” The abiding voice is one of gallingly insistent geewhiz positivity, accompanied by reiteration of the idea that boy oh boy are they ever some wild and crazy guys for making these just, y’know, totally out-there movies. Curiously, the tony words ‘Wesleyan University’ appear nowhere amid their self-mythologising.  
  
“Y’all got to learn to take care ‘a people smaller and sweeter than you,” Miss Bathsheeba tells the children - dialect and all - the kind of legend you might find burned into a ‘rustic’ wood plaque. Hushpuppy’s own revelations tend towards condolence-card homilies (“Everybody loses the thing that made them”) or morsels that might be ripped from the captions of one of Bil Keane’s ‘Family Circus’ cartoons (“When you’re small, you gotta fix what you can”).

The whole thing is worth a read

I like Matt Zoller Seitz a lot, but no review this overwritten has any credibility talking about the editing of a motion picture. Oppenheimer is a Chris Nolan picture and indeed, there's all the cinematic references and intertext, and it's all delightful. But what of it? All That Jazz? Really? (Ebert notoriously didn't like All That Jazz, but that's another story). In this story I believe we were spared - by Nolan and company - a scene where Oppie might have sung "Bye Bye Life" with Ben Vereen. This is neither a good nor a bad thing, but might have more to do with the fact that Oscar's appetite for musical comedy is notably thin. Dramatically, the chief interposition that explains all the attention to Oppenheimer's quirks is borrowed from Amadeus, in the form of Lewis Strauss's one-sided sense of rivalry. Strauss is self-consciously serious about serious things like science and freedom; but he's not much of a scientist. Oppenheimer is a brilliant scientist and by his accomplishments a great patriot, who in moments fulfills Strauss's vicarious dreams but is also a womanizer, friendly with Communists, and perhaps worst of all, he reacts to his great success not with pride but with shame and fear. There's so much Mozart and Salieri in this obsessive relationship that it simply has to be noted that Milos Forman already made that movie. 

Maybe we needed more "furiously entropic tendencies," and that is a hell of a final paragraph, but the last sentence makes two assertions, both are cliches, and neither is particularly accurate. Assertion #1: "We've been given the information but not told what to decide." That's just bullshit. The movie makes it clear enough that Oppenheimer's critics were jerks and backstabbers, even if (yes) it does show him in some compromising situations. Strauss is basically Salieri (and that's not unfair). Teller comes off as basically a psychotic pyromaniac (and that's not unfair either). President Truman is self-pitying, stoic, and as blind to Oppenheimer's pain as Patton slapping a shell-shocked solder. Anyone who stands in Oppenheimer's way gets nuked in this movie. And perhaps deservedly so, but spare us the nonsense that "Oppenheimer reports. You decide." The movie does give us Oppenheimer's mixed appraisal of the bomb and in conjunction with everything else, that's fascinating. When it doesn't break away from Oppenheimer, we see how he imagines the death the bomb will cause and it's at once a depiction of his extreme sensitivity and his extreme insularity. He never sees the Japanese who are actually killed. He sees his own mental image of death and devastation. (This was a controversy about the film, and I think the film should be defended for focusing on what Oppenheimer could have known or imagined). But the movie does break away from Oppenheimer frequently to satisfy its framing device. And it has mixed results. Strauss is interesting. But his downfall is dull and predictable. Yup, the scientists agree Strauss is an asshole. At least that wraps itself up more quickly than all the scenes about Oppenheimer's security clearance, which are standard McCarthy-era stuff except for one point where Oppenheimer's squeamishness about the bomb comes up.   
  
Z-S hasn't admitted to having seen Martin Ritt's film The Front, but that film ended with Woody Allen's character telling his inquisitors that "You can all fuck yourselves."  It was kind of a tacky ending but it had heart; and it was an answer to Elia Kazan's veiled admission "I'm glad what I done" (for naming names) on behalf of a crew and cast who had lived through the blacklist. Oppenheimer - whose alcoholism isn't seriously addressed - never had such a moment of clarity and it's not immediately apparent why, to some, but if he didn't want to be a part of the defense establishment (as you would understand if his guilt about the atom bomb ran so deep), why even try? There's a real answer there and the movie uses a lot of flim-flam and distraction to avoid dealing with it.  

Oliver Stone's JFK was also a feast of cinematography and editing and above all, distraction. It was justified because his movie was following a nutty DA through all of our doubts about a shocking event that was never explained to most people's satisfaction. Stone captured those thoughts and feelings, although it says more about us. Somehow, with all the people who hated Kennedy, it never occurred to any of us that an unstable, alienated person would make one more attempt to please the people around him? JFK was penance. 

So I don't agree that Oppenheimer leaves much up for us to decide, or that it gives us all the relevant information. The fact anyone could imagine it does causes me to doubt they even watched it. 

But the second issue is that the movie should leave conclusions up to the viewer. Z-S says it does; good for him. Then he says it should, and that's a cop-out. In a movie this fiercely didactic, maybe if you like it you should defend where it stands on the morality of the humans and the technology.

I wouldn't have reviewed Oppenheimer this highly. It has great parts and great ambitions but it's just as often cloying and desperate. And baffling that the moral ambiguity of the atom bomb wasn't enough. Maybe 3 stars for the movie, tops. And 2 for the review.
Thank you for introducing me to this. It's genuinely heartwarming to discover I'm not the only one who found Beasts of the Southern Wild unbearable.

You spend a lot of words entertaining reductive reasoning. “It’s like Amadeus” doesn’t actually mean anything. There’s not a genuine 1:1 comparison, it’s just something said that makes a discussion easier for those whose sole ingress into culture and history is cinema, rather than literature or archival research.

Not just that he's outright wrong on several aspects of the movie. Oppenheimer does see the effects of the bomb in Hiroshima and Nagasaki not just imagine it. There's a conference scene where they're looking at footage/pictures from the bombings and we get to see Oppenheimer reacting to those images.

They're also wrong about everyone opposing Oppenheimer getting "nuked" in the film. Lawrence for one was portrayed positively 😅. Even Strauss and Teller were allowed to give legitimate critiques towards Oppenheimer.
